Poor Richard’s Almanack

Also Read | Previous editions of OFFSIDE

Hello and welcome to another edition of Offside. Manchester United fans must feel like they are stuck in several Franz Kafka novels at the same time. Overnight, their league-winning club has metamorphosed into a giant, useless insect; successive managers are perpetually put on trial for the sins of an institution whose real architects never appear in the dock, while supporters, players and even managers are stuck in a constant circle of doom as invisible people in the castle grin on and rub their monies.But how did one of the world’s most popular clubs go from a perennial winner to a mid-table banter club?The answer lies with the Glazers, obviously, but even for that, we have to go a little further back to examine – to borrow a line from Churchill – the beginning of the end of Man Utd’s downfall. But before that, a small story about how the club was saved.Those familiar with United lore know that the club was saved thanks to a dog named The Major. Back in 1901, Newton Heath, as Manchester United was known, faced bankruptcy when The Major, who also happened to be the club’s mascot and belonged to captain Harry Stafford, went missing. The canine ended up at a restaurant where he was fancied by John Henry Davies for his little daughter's 12th birthday. The club captain refused to sell but later relented. But this chance meeting got John Henry Davies interested in the club’s fortunes, and he, along with other investors, saved it from bankruptcy and became its new chairman.And now United’s downfall, too, can be traced to another creature: a horse.Long before kings or presidents measured power by the size of their armies, nuclear arsenals or reverse tariffs, ancient Indian rulers had a rather ingenious way of establishing sovereignty: the. A consecrated horse would be allowed to wander across kingdoms with the king’s warriors, and anyone who stopped said horse was challenging the king’s power and claim to the land.The ritual features prominently in both Indian epics: theand the. In recorded history, Samudragupta also performed the ritual and commemorated it with gold coins. If the horse ritual was meant to cement a kingdom’s boundaries, in Manchester United’s case, its woes can be traced back to a stud named Rock of Gibraltar: the rock upon which modern Manchester United’s church was desecrated.Much like the sovereignty of Gibraltar has sullied Anglo-Spanish relations, Rock of Gibraltar’s ownership became a major bone of contention between Irish businessman John Magnier and his friend Sir Alex Ferguson.As Jonathan Wilson noted in his fantastic piece in, the unravelling began in the year of the Treble, when Mull of Kintyre, owned by Magnier, won the prestigious Gimcrack Stakes at York, which entailed giving a speech at the annual Gimcrack Dinner. Not wanting to replicate the plot of, Magnier asked his friend Sir Alex Ferguson to speak in his stead. But the racing establishment refused, saying only the horse’s owner would be allowed to show off said oratory.So Magnier made Ferguson the owner of another horse, Juniper (which also lost), and then Rock of Gibraltar, which won the race in 2001 and allowed Ferguson to give a speech.Like Manchester United in the nineties and noughties, Rock of Gibraltar turned out to be an extraordinarily successful racehorse, winning seven consecutive Group One races. His potential value as a breeding stallion skyrocketed, and Ferguson believed he was owed 50% of the horse’s future stud fees.An acrimonious legal battle followed with Magnier, and the club became entangled as well, with Magnier and his associate JP McManus selling their shares to one Malcolm Glazer in 2005, helping the Glazer family take Manchester United from a PLC to a private company.Now, speaking against Ferguson is the closest one can come in United’s religious order to blasphemy, and the only one brave enough to voice his dissent was the fallen Red Devil Roy Keane, who famously lashed out at Ferguson after his MUTV interview fallout and accused him of bringing his private life into the club with his argument with Magnier.Football finance expert Kieran Maguire once said during an interview with: "I think if that particular discussion over the horse had never taken place, we could be watching a very different Manchester United today. If that relationship had remained amicable, then Manchester United might not have been sold."But what’s done was done.During his tenure, Ferguson continued to defend the Glazers while racking up league wins and a Champions League, but the dark cloud of debt had already cast a pall over Old Trafford, and the dam broke the moment he retired.Now, if one is a fiscal dunce like yours truly, here’s a simple explainer of how the Glazers saddled United with debt.Malcolm Glazer bought Manchester United for approximately £790 million in 2005, but instead of paying for the club from his own pocket, he borrowed heavily and transferred the debt back onto the club.In financial parlance, it’s called a leveraged buyout. Football fans called it daylight robbery.From being virtually debt-free, United were suddenly £604 million in debt. Despite being the world’s most marketable club, those funds kept disappearing into the black hole to service the Glazers’ debt.A BBC Verify investigation found that approximately £1.19 billion left Manchester United between 2005 and 2024 in debt interest, debt repayments, dividends and fees associated with the takeover. Of that, £815 million went towards interest alone.To put that number in context, between 2009-10 and 2017-18, City, whose owners were coming up with imaginative ways of financial doping instead of suckling the club dry, had created an inflated revenue of £900 million.Ferguson’s managerial genius – which had transformed a relegation-hit club into modern football’s serial winners – continued to ensure no one needed to closely examine the increasingly fragile and mendacious edifice upon which Man Utd was built.Perhaps the problem lay with Ferguson himself, who essentially ran the entire club like a Sunday league team by doing a Kamal Haasan and playing every role himself.He wasn’t just the manager, but also chief strategist, final authority on recruitment and the institution’s footballing conscience.Once he was gone, the Glazers’ greatest sin became apparent, so much so that the managerial merry-go-round of the Abramovich era at Chelsea looked like an institution committed to long-term employment.The man handpicked by Ferguson, the Chosen One, David Moyes, quickly looked out of his depth before United tried every different managerial archetype.The man who was once congratulated on “inventing” modern football, Louis van Gaal, followed, and he came up short.Barcelona’s fallen angel José Mourinho, who almost succeeded Ferguson but chose to return to his beloved Chelsea after the fractious time at Real Madrid, failed to live up to his billing of a promised league title before his signature third-season meltdown.Ole Gunnar Solskjaer did give fans some nostalgic moments when the football was almost as good as the Fergie era before he was burdened with signings like Cristiano Ronaldo that upset the applecart.Erik ten Hag arrived as the next Dutch genius before Ruben Amorim’s 3-4-3 became synonymous with modern male suffering.Michael Carrick is only the latest manager to be handed the poisoned chalice, and it was quite clear that the fans didn’t blame him after the team lost 0-3 to a resurgent Bournemouth, which had just put Amorim’s AC Milan to the sword.After the game, the fans chanted “Sell United and f*** off home” before singing Michael Carrick’s song, just to make it clear who they blamed for United’s fortunes.Since Ferguson left, it has become evident that there is no rhyme or reason to hiring, with each manager putting together a smorgasbord of big-name footballers who would then be left behind like expensive vestigial organs for the next manager.United spent fortunes on Paul Pogba, Romelu Lukaku, Jadon Sancho, Antony, Harry Maguire and a succession of other footballers without developing anything resembling a coherent recruitment strategy.The problem was institutional rather than merely financial. The club had enough money to spend extravagantly, but its decision-making was so dysfunctional that extravagance became another form of self-harm.And this becomes particularly galling when one considers where Manchester United once stood in the financial hierarchy of European football.Before the Glazers darkened United’s door, United had topped Deloitte’s Football Money League for eight consecutive seasons. In 2026, they had fallen to eighth.Real Madrid were generating approximately €1.16 billion, Barcelona €975 million and Bayern Munich €861 million, while United managed €793 million. Liverpool had also overtaken them, becoming the highest-earning English club.The comparison with Madrid is instructive because it is perhaps the only club that has a global fanbase to match United’s. The club is owned by members who elect the club’s president. Florentino Pérez might behave like a European emperor collectingthe way Caesars collected gladiators, but he’s accountable to a membership structure, and the club’s profits are reinvested rather than distributed to private shareholders.Real Madrid have borrowed heavily to renovate the Santiago Bernabéu, but the crucial difference is what the debt finances. Madrid's borrowing has helped transform their stadium into a commercial powerhouse, generating revenue from football, hospitality and other events. By 2025-26, Madrid reported annual revenue of €1.22 billion, with stadium revenues more than doubling compared with the period before redevelopment.United's debt, by contrast, helped finance the purchase of United.Bayern Munich offer another example.Under Germany's 50+1 system, the members' association retains control, owning 75% of Bayern's football company, while Adidas, Audi and Allianz own the remainder.And then there is Liverpool, whose American owners, Fenway Sports Group, have managed to achieve something the Glazers apparently considered impossible: owning a Premier League football club without making every major decision an expensive exercise in institutional masochism.Meanwhile, the club’s once-vaunted infrastructure was in ruins.Cristiano Ronaldo was horrified by the gym facilities.Robbie Savage savaged them as being on par with a League One team.And Zlatan was aghast at the club’s “small mentality” when he was docked one quid from his wage packet because he dared raid the minibar at a hotel for a bottle of juice.Old Trafford became a living monument to the Glazers’ greed. While Real Madrid rebuilt the Bernabéu and Tottenham constructed an enormous modern stadium, United's stadium became known for being as leaky as its defence.And then appeared some light at the end of the horizon: Jim Ratcliffe, one of the UK’s richest men, acquired 29.4% from the Glazers and ostensibly took charge of its footballing operations.United acquired another layer of management, and soon we got a glimpse of what increased corporatisation does to a footballing institution.Dan Ashworth was brought in as sporting director and then let go five months later, which cost the club a pretty £4.1 million, excluding his wages.Huge amounts were also spent on golden handshakes for Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim.He also started the practice of getting executives from the blue half of Manchester, including Omar Berrada as chief executive, Jason Wilcox as director of football, Sam Erith as head of performance, Toby Craig as communications chief and Stephen Torpey to run the academy, leading Nicky Butt to complain: “Every City staff member goes to Man Utd now.” He pointed out that Real Madrid would hardly attempt the same experiment with Barcelona.And many of them were operating at City at a time when the club engaged in systemic financial doping, using sham commercial arrangements to inflate revenues and understate costs.And those who bore the brunt of Ratcliffe’s financial tightening – which perhaps explains his disdain for migrants – were United’s staff, as he scrapped free lunches, reduced benefits, increased ticket pricing and also scaled back support for the Manchester United Foundation. And he also nixed Ferguson’s role as Global Ambassador.But perhaps Ratcliffe’s starkest failure was the player recruitment, or lack thereof, this season.After exorcising Ruben Amorim’s 3-4-3, interim first-team manager Carrick got Manchester United playing out of their skin to reach third in the league, picking up more points than any other manager this season. He did it with a style of counter-attacking football and by getting the best out of his team, but it was obvious that would fail the second-season test.United needed reinforcements, more so because of the added pressure of Champions League games.The club failed to sign a left-back despite Luke Shaw’s history of spending time in the treatment room, didn’t get a proper centre-forward, leaving Benjamin Šeško as the most recognisable out-and-out striker, and were outspent by newly promoted teams, leaving Carrick to wonder where the added funds from qualifying for Europe went.Alas, it’s one in a long line of questions that everyone associated with the red half of Manchester has about how United will get out of its post-Fergie funk, with no clear answers.In, Benjamin Franklin wrote in 1758: “For want of a nail the shoe was lost; for want of a shoe the horse was lost; and for want of a horse the rider was lost, being overtaken and slain by the enemy, all for want of care about a horse-shoe nail.”And we can now add a Fergie post-script: “And for the want of a horse, a club was lost.”A dog saved Manchester United many years ago. A horse might be the reason it was lost.1. Sir Alex Ferguson’s new book 'Games of My Life' is a cruel time machine for Man Utd fans 2. Why Sir Alex Ferguson vs Pep Guardiola is no longer a debate 3. Article Title: 'I apologize to everyone my words have upset': Kylian Mbappé reacts to 'Chinese dictator' controversy
Article Text:

Brands End Partnerships With Mbappé

Social media backlash grows

Kylian Mbappé has apologised after comments about a meme featuring Chinese revolutionary leader Mao Zedong sparked anger in China. The controversy has also cost the French football star partnerships with three Chinese companies, while criticism of his remarks spread across Chinese social media.“My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world,” Mbappé said in a statement Tuesday.“I apologize to everyone my words have upset," he said. "This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry."Chinese beverage company Dongpeng, dairy producer Mengniu and cheese maker Milkground announced on Tuesday that they were ending their agreements with the footballer. All three companies issued similar statements opposing “any words and actions that hurt national sentiment”.The decisions followed the circulation of a video on X that appeared to show Mbappé discussing his favourite internet meme during an interview ahead of his appearance on the French online talk show The Bridge.Asked about the meme, Mbappé described it as “a video someone made of a guy ... I think he was a Chinese dictator”.The clip then showed an edited image placing his face on the body of Mao Zedong.Football fans often jokingly portray Mbappé as a dictator in online memes because of his larger-than-life presence in the sport. However, Mao remains a sensitive historical figure in China.He led the Communist Party to victory in the Chinese civil war and founded the People's Republic of China in 1949. While many still revere him, his rule also included disastrous policies, including the Great Leap Forward, which contributed to a famine that killed an estimated 30 million people.China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun also commented on the controversy, saying that “words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society.”Social media platform RedNote said its content partnership with Mbappé had ended on December 31, 2024, and announced it would “remove related promotional materials.” His account was also blocked from gaining new followers.Meanwhile, hashtags calling for boycotts and reporting the brands' decisions topped Weibo's trending charts, with some users criticising Mbappé and urging him not to visit China.
Article Summary: Kylian Mbappé apologises after comments about a meme featuring Mao Zedong. French football star's remarks have sparked anger in China. Three Chinese companies have ended partnerships with the footballer. Chinese social media users have called for boycotts and urged him not to visit China.

Article Title: Ballon d'Or explained: Who votes, how are points awarded and how is the winner chosen?
Article Text:
Harry Kane and Alexia Putellas (Image credit: X)

Here is a look at how the

Ballon d'Or voting process

works:

Who votes for the Ballon d'Or?

Sports journalists vote to choose the Ballon d'Or winner.

For the men's award, one journalist each from 100 countries can vote. These countries are selected based on the FIFA men's rankings as of September 8, 2026.

For the women's award, journalists from 50 countries can vote, based on the FIFA women's rankings.

Each journalist picks 10 players from a list of 30 nominees and ranks them from first to 10th.

The player ranked first gets the most points, while the player ranked 10th gets the fewest.

All the points are added together. The player with the highest total wins the award.

How are the 30 Ballon d'Or nominees selected?

The editorial teams of France Football magazine and L'Equipe help select the 30 nominees.

For the men's award, the selection process also includes at least one member of the previous year's jury and UEFA ambassadors Luis Figo and Fabio Capello.

Nadine Kessler is involved in selecting nominees for the women's award.

Once the shortlist is ready, the eligible journalists vote to decide the winner.

How does the Ballon d'Or points system work?

The points are awarded as follows:

Rank Points 1st 15 2nd 12 3rd 10 4th 8 5th 7 6th 5 7th 4 8th 3 9th 2 10th 1

What happens if players finish level on points?

If two players get the same total points, the player with more first-place votes wins.

If they have the same number of first-place votes, their second-place votes are compared.

This process continues until a winner is decided.

Who selects the 30 Ballon d'Or nominees?

The editorial teams of France Football magazine and L'Equipe help select the 30 nominees.

For the men's award, the selection process also includes at least one member of the previous year's jury and UEFA ambassadors Luis Figo and Fabio Capello.

Nadine Kessler is involved in selecting nominees for the women's award.

Once the final list is ready, eligible sports journalists vote to decide the winner.

NEW DELHI: The Ballon d'Or is one of football's most prestigious individual awards. Every year, the honour is given to a player who has impressed with their performances during the season. But the winner is not decided by goals or trophies alone. Sports journalists vote to choose the player who deserves the award.Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or on Monday after a remarkable season with Bayern Munich and England. He scored 61 goals in 51 matches for Bayern across all competitions, helping the German club win the domestic league and cup double.Kane became the first Englishman to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001. Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas won the women's Ballon d'Or for the third time.So, how is the winner chosen? Who gets to vote, and how are the points calculated?The points a player receives depend on where each journalist places them on their ballot. A player ranked first receives the highest number of points, while the player ranked 10th gets the lowest.
Article Summary: Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or on Monday after a remarkable season with Bayern Munich. Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas won the women's award for the third time. Sports journalists vote to choose the player who deserves the award.

Article Title: Who is Alexia Putellas? All you need to know about Spain's three-time Ballon d'Or winner
Article Text:

Who is Alexia Putellas ?

What did Putellas say after winning her third Ballon d'Or?

Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for a record-equalling third time on Monday after an impressive 2025-26 season with Barcelona.The 32-year-old helped Barcelona win four trophies, including the Women's Champions League, before leaving her childhood club to join Women's Super League (WSL) side London City Lionesses in July.Putellas also played a key role in Spain's success in the Women's Nations League last December. Her latest award puts her alongside former Barcelona teammate Aitana Bonmati, who won the honour in 2023, 2024 and 2025.Putellas had previously claimed the award in 2021 and 2022. Her latest victory marks a remarkable comeback after a serious knee injury threatened to derail her career.Born in Mollet del Valles, a town near Barcelona in Spain's Catalonia region, Putellas grew up playing football on the streets. She soon became a Barcelona fan and regularly watched matches at Camp Nou.She admired former Barcelona and Spain midfielder Andres Iniesta, along with Brazilian stars Rivaldo and Ronaldinho. Her early football journey included a summer camp run by former Barcelona midfielder Xavi and spells with local club CE Sabadell.Putellas later joined Barcelona's famous La Masia academy for a year before moving to Espanyol and Levante. She returned to Barcelona in 2012, beginning a long association with the club she had supported since childhood.During her 14 years at Barcelona, she won 38 trophies, including 10 league titles and four European Cups. She also earned the nickname 'La Reina', which means 'The Queen'.Putellas first won the Ballon d'Or Feminin in 2021 and successfully defended the award in 2022. However, her career suffered a major setback when she tore her anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) just before the European Championship that year. The injury ruled her out of the tournament and kept her away from her best form for some time. Although she won the Ballon d'Or again in 2022, she had a limited role in Spain's 2023 Women's World Cup-winning campaign.Putellas gradually returned to her best. She scored in the 2024 Women's Champions League final and continued to improve the following season.In 2025-26, she took on greater responsibility in Barcelona's attack while Bonmati was sidelined for five months with an injury. Putellas helped the club win four trophies and finished the campaign with 21 goals and 13 assists across all competitions.She also scored twice in Spain's 4-0 victory over England in June, a result that secured Spain's place at the 2027 Women's World Cup.Putellas used her latest success to encourage young players around the world to follow their dreams, regardless of their gender or background."All the boys and girls around the world - if you love football and if you want to play football, play football. It doesn't matter if you're a boy or if you're a girl," Putellas said as quoted by BBC."Doesn't matter where you come from. Don't listen if someone tells you, you can't do it. Believe in yourself."
Article Summary: Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for a record- equalling third time. The 32-year-old helped Barcelona win four trophies, including the Women's Champions League. Her latest victory marks a remarkable comeback after a serious knee injury threatened to derail her career.

Article Title: Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d’Or, ends England’s 25-year wait and makes history as first player to win two individual awards in one night
Article Text:
Soccer Football - Ballon d'Or - London Palladium, London, Britain - October 26, 2026 Bayern Munich's Harry Kane celebrates after winning the men's Ballon d'Or award Action Images via Reuters/Matthew Childs

Kane ends England’s 25-year Ballon d’Or wait

Harry Kane Kylian Mbappé Lamine Yamal Rodri Lionel Messi Khvicha Kvaratskhelia Ousmane Dembélé Erling Haaland Michael Olise Fabián Ruiz

Bayern’s 61 goals explain the scale of his season

Bayern Munich forward Harry Kane at the Golden Boot award ceremony for Europe's top scorer, in Munich, Germany, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026. (Christoph Lother/dpa via AP)

The Gerd Müller Trophy makes it a historic double

England’s record scorer is closing in on another landmark

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

England's Harry Kane (9) celebrates after scoring a goal during the World Cup Group L soccer match between England and Croatia in Arlington, Texas, near Dallas, Wednesday, June 17, 2026. (AP Photo/Tony Gutierrez)

Harry Kane has spent years chasing the biggest prizes in football, and his latest achievement has taken him somewhere no player has reached before. The Bayern Munich striker has won the 2026 Ballon d’Or, ending a 25-year wait for an English winner, while also claiming the Gerd Müller Trophy at the same ceremony. His 73 goals for club and country made the case, with the resulting double giving an extraordinary season an equally historic finish.The Leytonstone-born forward becomes the fifth Englishman to win the men’s Ballon d’Or, following Sir Stanley Matthews in 1956, Sir Bobby Charlton in 1966, Kevin Keegan in 1978 and 1979, and Michael Owen in 2001. Kane’s seventh Ballon d’Or nomination proved to be the charm, with the Bayern Munich striker finally claiming the coveted prize after years of falling short amid a lack of major team trophies. His victory ends England’s 25-year wait for a winner and makes him the first player to collect the award as a Bayern Munich player.Matthews was the inaugural winner when the prize was introduced in 1956, while Keegan remains the only Englishman to win it twice and the only one to claim it in consecutive years. Keegan also previously held the distinction of being the only English winner playing for a foreign club, having collected both awards while representing Hamburg in Germany.Kane’s 2026 triumph follows a season in which he scored 73 goals across 65 competitive appearances for Bayern and England, alongside eight assists. He finished with the second-highest single-season goal tally by a player in the 21st century, averaging more than a goal per appearance across the campaign.The final men’s Ballon d’Or rankings placed Kylian Mbappé second and Lamine Yamal third, while Lionel Messi ended the night in fifth.The final top 10:Kane was joined in the winners’ spotlight by his female counterpart, Alexia Putellas, who won the 2026 Ballon d’Or Féminin. The Barcelona legend claimed the women’s prize for a record-equalling third time, following her victories in 2021 and 2022, keeping the award in Spanish hands for a sixth consecutive year.Putellas was rewarded for a spectacular 2025–26 campaign with Barcelona Femení, captaining the club to a historic quadruple that included the UEFA Women’s Champions League, before moving to London City Lionesses.Kane’s club campaign supplied the largest share of his remarkable total, with 61 goals and seven assists across 51 appearances for Bayern in all competitions. His Bundesliga record was particularly striking: he scored 36 times in 31 appearances, including 26 starts, at a rate of one goal every 66.1 minutes.He carried that finishing into Europe, scoring 14 goals in 13 Champions League appearances as Bayern reached the semi-finals, while also contributing two assists in the competition. His domestic cup campaign proved even more prolific, with 10 goals in six DFB-Pokal appearances as Bayern secured their 21st triumph in the competition, including a hat-trick from Kane in the final against Stuttgart.He also scored once in one appearance in the Franz Beckenbauer Supercup, completing a season in which his goals came across every major competition Bayern contested. His combined rate of one goal or assist every 59 minutes reflected how frequently he influenced matches, whether by finishing moves himself or creating opportunities for teammates.The season also brought Kane a second European Golden Shoe and the Bundesliga’s Torjägerkanone for the third consecutive campaign, reinforcing his position as the division’s leading scorer. His individual recognition now extends beyond those domestic honours, with the Ballon d’Or placing him at the top of world football’s annual individual rankings.Kane’s second award on the night was the Gerd Müller Trophy, which recognises the leading goalscorer across club and international football during a European season. Introduced in 2021 as the Striker of the Year award, it was renamed in 2022 to honour the legendary German forward, who died in 2021.Kane had already won the trophy in 2024 and collected it again in 2026, but adding the main Ballon d’Or created a first in the ceremony’s history. No player had previously won two individual awards during the same Ballon d’Or gala, although organisers had confirmed that the rules permitted multiple honours because each award is decided through a separate voting process.The possibility had been there, but Kane’s 73-goal campaign turned it into reality, making him the first player to claim both prizes at one ceremony. His achievement also gives the Gerd Müller Trophy a different significance, moving beyond recognition for goals alone to accompany the sport’s most prestigious individual award.Kane’s contribution to England’s season further strengthened his case, with 12 international goals taking his career tally for the national team to 91. He became England’s record goalscorer in 2024, and his latest run has brought the century mark within reach.Six of those goals came at the 2026 World Cup, where three were match-winners and Kane overtook Gary Lineker to become England’s leading scorer in World Cup finals. Lineker himself had been nominated for the Ballon d’Or five times, adding another historical connection to Kane’s latest achievement.During the period used to assess the Striker of the Year award, Kane scored for England every 97.7 minutes. Since September 2025, he has also accounted for 32.4 per cent of England’s goals in matches he played, underlining how central he remains to the national side’s attack.At 33, Kane has now collected the Ballon d’Or, the Gerd Müller Trophy, another European Golden Shoe and a third consecutive Bundesliga scoring title in a season that has reshaped his place in football history. England’s wait for another winner is over, and no player has ever left a Ballon d’Or ceremony with the same two individual honours that Kane has claimed.
Article Summary: Harry Kane has won the 2026 Ballon d’Or, ending a 25-year wait for an English winner. The Bayern Munich striker also claimed the Gerd Müller Trophy at the same ceremony. The Leytonstone-born forward becomes the fifth Englishman to win the men’s prize.
